newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS-Italy markets keep nerve on German asset row.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Italy markets keep nerve on German asset row.

text.p: Italian financial markets kept their nerve on Thursday, after a clash between the Bundesbank and the German government over Bonn's plans to revalue assets ahead of EMU, and initially judged that Italy's chances of joining the single currency had improved.

But the market remained concerned about the conflict and economists said government bond and lira investors were waiting to see if French Socialists won Sunday's parliamentary election runoff before making any big decisions.

Italian government bonds (Btps) and the lira wobbled near levels they closed at on Wednesday, just before the Bundesbank announced it rejected Bonn's plan to revalue gold reserves to give the public finances a much-needed boost.

By 1040 GMT the lira was at 990.45 per mark and the June Btp futures contract on LIFFE 24 basis points down at 128.89. The yield on the 10-year benchmark Btp was 140 basis points above that on the benchmark Bund, unchanged from Wednesday.

"The markets are taking the view that this (Buba-Bonn dispute) doesn't affect the view EMU will go ahead on time in 1999 but the chances of broader EMU membership are more likely," said Robert Prior, economist at HSBC in London.

Economists say the strong political will to launch European economic and monetary union (EMU) will override strict adherence to EMU criteria, and that increases the chances Italy will be in the first wave of nations forming a single currency in 1999.

Providing EMU looks like going ahead on time, they say, Italian markets will not suffer as investors believe Italy will maintain its drive for fiscal prudence and the convergence process will continue.
But many unknown factors muddied the outlook and traders said as markets opened they had been confused at the significance of the German issue and the bond market was tense.

Parts of Germany were on holiday on Thursday, so dealers expected little news to clarify the outcome of the Bundesbank's decision and said instead investors would return to focusing on the election in France.
Here economists saw even greater cause for concern.
"What is more important for Italy's prospects in EMU is whether the Socialists take control," said Pio De Gregorio, economist at NatWest Markets in Milan.
"The risk is the Socialists ask for a more flexible reading of Maastricht requirements and the markets anticipate the euro will not be as strong as the Bundesbank would like," he said.
Broadly, this would create a stronger dollar against European currencies including the lira, he added.

The Socialists are also keener to have Italy and Spain in EMU at the start, while the Bundesbank and the German public are seen preferring Italy entering later once it has established longer-term economic credentials.
Prior said a key risk derived from Italy being seen as a primary EMU member. This could provoke adverse reactions in Germany and prompt the whole process to be delayed.
Delay would, in turn, fuel concern EMU could be shelved, removing any incentive for Italy to maintain its fiscal rigour, he said.
That uncertainty and the wait for the Italian government's three-year economic plan due on Friday, are seen likely to keep Italian markets jittery for the next few trading sessions.

But traders and analysts, reluctant to make any numerical predictions in such a confused market, said they doubted either bonds or the lira will move much before the result of the French vote in known.
